lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
If we want to multiply one square matrix by another (which has the same dimensions), we multiply each row in the first matrix by each column in the second.

Content:
For example, suppose we want to multiply two matrices
[MATH: A = \left\lbrack
\matrix {
1 & 6 \
4 & 3
}
\right\rbrack]
and
[MATH: B = \left\lbrack
\matrix {
-3 & 0 \
2 & -5
}
\right\rbrack.]

Content:
The matrices [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] are both [MATH: 2 \times 2] matrices, and their product will be another [MATH: 2 \times 2] matrix [MATH: C,] as follows:

Content:
[MATH: \eqalign {
\underbrace{
\left\lbrack
\matrix {
1 & 6 \
4 & 3
}
\right\rbrack}_{A}

\underbrace{
\left\lbrack
\matrix {
-3 & 0 \
2 & -5
}
\right\rbrack}_{B}

&=
\underbrace{
\left\lbrack
\matrix {
\ast & \ast \
\ast & \ast
}
\right\rbrack
}_{C}
}]
Now, we calculate the entries of [MATH: C] (shown as [MATH: \ast]'s in the equation above).

Content:
To find [MATH: c_{11},] the entry at the intersection of the 1st row and 1st column, we calculate the dot product of the 1st row of [MATH: A] and the 1st column of [MATH: B\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: \eqalign {
\left\lbrack
\matrix {
\color{blue}{1} & \color{blue}{6} \
4 & 3
}
\right\rbrack

\left\lbrack
\matrix {
\color{red}{-3} & 0 \
\color{red}{2} & -5
}
\right\rbrack

&=
\left\lbrack
\matrix {
{\color{blue}{1}} \cdot ({\color{red}{-3}}) + {\color{blue}{6}} \cdot {\color{red}{2}} & \ast \
\ast & \ast
}
\right\rbrack

= \left\lbrack
\matrix {
9 & \ast \
\ast & \ast
}
\right\rbrack
}]

Content:
To find [MATH: c_{12},] the entry at the intersection of the 1st row and 2nd column, we calculate the dot product of the 1st row of [MATH: A] and the 2nd column of [MATH: B\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: \eqalign {
\left\lbrack
\matrix {
\color{blue}{1} & \color{blue}{6} \
4 & 3
}
\right\rbrack

\left\lbrack
\matrix {
-3 & \color{red}{0} \
2 & \color{red}{-5}
}
\right\rbrack

&=
\left\lbrack
\matrix {
9 & {\color{blue}{1}} \cdot {\color{red}{0}} + {\color{blue}{6}} \cdot ({\color{red}{-5}}) \
\ast & \ast
}
\right\rbrack

= \left\lbrack
\matrix {
9 & -30 \
\ast & \ast
}
\right\rbrack
}]

Content:
To find [MATH: c_{21},] the entry at the intersection of the 2nd row and 1st column, we calculate the dot product of the 2nd row of [MATH: A] and the 1st column of [MATH: B\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: \eqalign {
\left\lbrack
\matrix {
{1} & {6} \
\color{blue}{4} & \color{blue}{3}
}
\right\rbrack

\left\lbrack
\matrix {
\color{red}{-3} & 0 \
\color{red}{2} & -5
}
\right\rbrack

&=
\left\lbrack
\matrix {
9 & -30 \
{\color{blue}{4}} \cdot ({\color{red}{-3}}) + {\color{blue}{3}} \cdot {\color{red}{2}} & \ast
}
\right\rbrack

= \left\lbrack
\matrix {
9 & -30 \
-6 & \ast
}
\right\rbrack
}]

Content:
To find [MATH: c_{22},] the entry at the intersection of the 2nd row and 2nd column, we calculate the dot product of the 2nd row of [MATH: A] and the 2nd column of [MATH: B\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: \eqalign {
\left\lbrack
\matrix {
{1} & {6} \
\color{blue}{4} & \color{blue}{3}
}
\right\rbrack

\left\lbrack
\matrix {
-3 & \color{red}{0} \
2 & \color{red}{-5}
}
\right\rbrack

&=
\left\lbrack
\matrix {
9 & -30 \
-6 & {\color{blue}{4}} \cdot {\color{red}{0}} + {\color{blue}{3}} \cdot ({\color{red}{-5}})
}
\right\rbrack

= \left\lbrack
\matrix {
9 & -30 \
-6 & -15
}
\right\rbrack
}]

Content:
Therefore, our final answer is

Content:
[MATH: \eqalign {
\left\lbrack
\matrix {
{1} & {6} \
4 & 3
}
\right\rbrack

\left\lbrack
\matrix {
-3 & 0 \
2 & -5
}
\right\rbrack

= \left\lbrack
\matrix {
9 & -30 \
-6 & -15
}
\right\rbrack.
}]

Item 2 — Example: Multiplying 2x2 Square Matrices

Example Prompt:
Find [MATH: AB] and [MATH: BA,] if
[MATH: [1|0; − 5|1]]
and
[MATH: [0|1; − 1|2]]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Multiplying each row in the first matrix by each column in the second, we get

[MATH: AB|= [1|0; − 5|1][0|1; − 1|2]; = [1 ⋅ 0 + 0 ⋅ (− 1)|1 ⋅ 1 + 0 ⋅ 2; − 5 ⋅ 0 + 1 ⋅ (− 1)|− 5 ⋅ 1 + 1 ⋅ 2]; = [0|1; − 1|− 3]]

and

[MATH: BA|= [0|1; − 1|2][1|0; − 5|1]; = [0 ⋅ 1 + 1 ⋅ (− 5)|0 ⋅ 0 + 1 ⋅ 1; − 1 ⋅ 1 + 2 ⋅ (− 5)|− 1 ⋅ 0 + 2 ⋅ 1]; = [− 5|1; − 11|2].]

Watch out! Notice that
[MATH: AB \neq BA.]
Matrix multiplication is not commutative, meaning that when we switch the order of multiplication, we often get a different result (like we did in this example).
